messages.subject: distsamp, density estimation
parts:
Hello,

I am using the distsamp function in Unmarked to estimate the density of three species of monkeys in a given area. I basically need some help reading my results as I am very much a beginner.

I have chosen the halfnorm detection function as it had the lowest AIC. Then I go on to write my null model: 

fm1.2 <- distsamp(~1 ~1, umf2, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",
                unitsOut="kmsq")

and back transform it to see what my density without taking into account the covariates:

 backTransform(fm1.2, type="state") 
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Density estimate(s)

 Estimate  SE LinComb (Intercept)
     4.69 1.6    1.55           1

Transformation: exp 

Having found the covariates which explain my density (distance to all roads) and detection (NDVI level) best, I then backtransform again and receive a new density. What does this mean? Why do I have two densities and which one should I use? 

fm10.2 <- distsamp(~ndvi_scaled ~allroads_scaled, umf2, keyfun="halfnorm", output="density",
                 unitsOut="kmsq")

> backTransform(linearComb(fm10.2['state'], c(0, 1)))
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Density estimate(s)

 Estimate    SE LinComb (Intercept) allroads_scaled
     2.02 0.384   0.705           0               1

Transformation: exp 

At the moment both of these densities seem too high so I think I might have done something wrong. This species is predicted to have <500 individuals within a 343kmsq area. Any help would be really appreciated. If you need more information off me, please let me know.

Many thanks

Emily

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] distsamp, density estimation
parts:
hi Emily, can you show the summary of the two models?
 I assume the distance is measured in meters right?
 Can you show a histogram of the distance measurements?
 In the 2nd use of backTransform it looks like you're setting the intercept to 0 and the coefficient on roads to 1, so maybe that's not what you want to do.
regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] distsamp, density estimation
parts:
hi Emily,
So I think the first model implies that the density of monkeys is 

> exp(1.55)
[1] 4.71147 monkeys/ km^2

That's a lot of monkeys I guess -- way higher than your expectation I guess, but I think the calculation is probably correct.   To better understand this it would be useful to know: (a) how many monkeys were observed? (looks like n = 16 to me) and (b) what was the total TRANSECT AREA that was surveyed?   I think you can calibrate the estimate of 4.7 pretty well by looking at the empirical density of observed individuals. I notice that the detection distance is only out to about 35 m, so as a crude naive estimate you can take your transect length, multiply it by 70, and then get an estimated density by 16/[transect length * 70] . I'd be curious to see what that number is.  Can you compute that and send it?

As for the 2nd model with the roads covariate -- you should use the predict() function and make a prediction of density on EACH transect, using the actual road covariate value for that transect.

regards
andy
